question: What does the hydraulic grade line represent at a point in a pressurised water main?
correctAnswer: The elevation head plus the pressure head at that point
explanation: The hydraulic grade line combines elevation head and pressure head, so its height above a point shows the pressure available there.
options: The elevation of the pipe centreline only
The elevation head plus the pressure head at that point
The velocity head in the main only
The ground surface elevation above the main
optionA: The elevation of the pipe centreline only
optionB: The elevation head plus the pressure head at that point
optionC: The velocity head in the main only
optionD: The ground surface elevation above the main
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Hydraulic Grade Interpretation. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Two taps are on the same pressure zone with the same hydraulic grade. Why does the higher tap show lower pressure?
correctAnswer: Less of the total head remains as pressure head at the higher elevation
explanation: Total head is shared between elevation and pressure. More elevation head leaves less pressure head at the same hydraulic grade.
options: The higher tap has a larger service pipe
The water is older at the higher tap
Less of the total head remains as pressure head at the higher elevation
The hydraulic grade rises at the higher tap
optionA: The higher tap has a larger service pipe
optionB: The water is older at the higher tap
optionC: Less of the total head remains as pressure head at the higher elevation
optionD: The hydraulic grade rises at the higher tap
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Hydraulic Grade Interpretation. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: During a period of high demand, the hydraulic grade line in a feeder main slopes more steeply toward the far end of the zone. What does the steeper slope indicate?
correctAnswer: Greater head loss per unit length from higher flow
explanation: The slope of the hydraulic grade line reflects head loss along the pipe, and head loss increases as flow increases.
options: Greater head loss per unit length from higher flow
A closed valve at the start of the zone
Rising storage levels in the zone
Lower friction in the feeder main
optionA: Greater head loss per unit length from higher flow
optionB: A closed valve at the start of the zone
optionC: Rising storage levels in the zone
optionD: Lower friction in the feeder main
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Hydraulic Grade Interpretation. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A pressure gauge at a hydrant reads the same as the elevation difference between the hydrant and the reservoir water surface, converted to pressure. What condition does this describe?
correctAnswer: Static conditions with no flow in the main
explanation: With no flow there is no friction loss, so pressure is set only by the elevation difference to the source water level.
options: Peak hour demand in the zone
A pump running at full speed
Active flushing near the hydrant
Static conditions with no flow in the main
optionA: Peak hour demand in the zone
optionB: A pump running at full speed
optionC: Active flushing near the hydrant
optionD: Static conditions with no flow in the main
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Hydraulic Grade Interpretation. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: An operator compares a measured pressure with the pressure predicted from the hydraulic grade. The measured value is much lower during flow. What is the most likely explanation?
correctAnswer: Head loss in the main is greater than expected, possibly from a restriction or partially closed valve
explanation: A larger than expected drop between the hydraulic grade and the measured pressure points to extra head loss in the system.
options: The reservoir level has risen above normal
The service line is oversized for the building
Head loss in the main is greater than expected, possibly from a restriction or partially closed valve
Air has been fully removed from the main
optionA: The reservoir level has risen above normal
optionB: The service line is oversized for the building
optionC: Head loss in the main is greater than expected, possibly from a restriction or partially closed valve
optionD: Air has been fully removed from the main
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Hydraulic Grade Interpretation. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: What is the main purpose of a pressure reducing valve in a distribution system?
correctAnswer: To hold downstream pressure at a set value that is lower than the upstream pressure
explanation: A pressure reducing valve throttles flow so downstream pressure stays at the chosen setting despite higher upstream pressure.
options: To hold downstream pressure at a set value that is lower than the upstream pressure
To increase flow to a higher pressure zone
To remove air from a high point in a main
To measure flow between two pressure zones
optionA: To hold downstream pressure at a set value that is lower than the upstream pressure
optionB: To increase flow to a higher pressure zone
optionC: To remove air from a high point in a main
optionD: To measure flow between two pressure zones
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pressure Management And PRVs. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Why do utilities lower excessive pressure in a zone where leakage is a concern?
correctAnswer: Leakage flow generally increases as pressure increases, so lower pressure reduces water loss
explanation: Leak openings discharge more water at higher pressure, so managing pressure down reduces background leakage and break frequency.
options: Lower pressure makes leaks easier to hear
Lower pressure increases the life of hydrants only
Leakage is unrelated to pressure in a zone
Leakage flow generally increases as pressure increases, so lower pressure reduces water loss
optionA: Lower pressure makes leaks easier to hear
optionB: Lower pressure increases the life of hydrants only
optionC: Leakage is unrelated to pressure in a zone
optionD: Leakage flow generally increases as pressure increases, so lower pressure reduces water loss
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pressure Management And PRVs. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A pressure reducing valve station includes a smaller bypass valve in parallel with the main valve. What is the purpose of the smaller valve?
correctAnswer: To handle low flows accurately when demand is small
explanation: A small valve controls low flows more stably, while the large valve opens when demand rises beyond the small valve range.
options: To supply the zone during a fire only
To handle low flows accurately when demand is small
To drain the downstream main for repair
To raise pressure at night in the zone
optionA: To supply the zone during a fire only
optionB: To handle low flows accurately when demand is small
optionC: To drain the downstream main for repair
optionD: To raise pressure at night in the zone
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pressure Management And PRVs. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: After a pressure reducing valve is serviced, what should the operator confirm before returning the station to normal service?
correctAnswer: That downstream pressure matches the set point under flowing and no flow conditions
explanation: Checking the set point under both conditions confirms the valve controls properly and does not allow pressure creep at low demand.
options: That downstream pressure matches the set point under flowing and no flow conditions
That upstream pressure has been raised to its maximum
That all zone valves downstream are fully closed
That the bypass is left open at all times
optionA: That downstream pressure matches the set point under flowing and no flow conditions
optionB: That upstream pressure has been raised to its maximum
optionC: That all zone valves downstream are fully closed
optionD: That the bypass is left open at all times
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pressure Management And PRVs. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A zone supplied through a pressure reducing valve reports rising night pressures over several weeks. What should be checked first?
correctAnswer: The valve and its pilot system for wear, debris, or a failing seat
explanation: Pressure creep at low flow is a classic sign that the valve is not seating or its pilot controls need attention.
options: The chlorine residual at the zone entry point
The accuracy of the zone master meter
The condition of hydrant caps in the zone
The valve and its pilot system for wear, debris, or a failing seat
optionA: The chlorine residual at the zone entry point
optionB: The accuracy of the zone master meter
optionC: The condition of hydrant caps in the zone
optionD: The valve and its pilot system for wear, debris, or a failing seat
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pressure Management And PRVs. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A district metered area is created by closing boundary valves and metering all inflows. What is the main benefit of this arrangement?
correctAnswer: Leakage and consumption in that area can be quantified and compared over time
explanation: Metering a defined area lets operators track its water balance and spot changes that indicate new leakage.
options: Chlorine residual in the area no longer needs monitoring
Leakage and consumption in that area can be quantified and compared over time
The area can be removed from the sampling program
Pressure in the area becomes independent of the rest of the system
optionA: Chlorine residual in the area no longer needs monitoring
optionB: Leakage and consumption in that area can be quantified and compared over time
optionC: The area can be removed from the sampling program
optionD: Pressure in the area becomes independent of the rest of the system
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: District Metered Areas. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Minimum night flow in a district metered area rises steadily over a month while customer use is unchanged. What is the best interpretation?
correctAnswer: A new leak or an increase in background leakage is likely in the area
explanation: Night flow is mostly leakage plus small legitimate use, so a rising trend with stable use points to growing leakage.
options: The boundary valves are fully closed and sealed
Customer meters in the area are reading more accurately
A new leak or an increase in background leakage is likely in the area
Storage in the area is turning over faster
optionA: The boundary valves are fully closed and sealed
optionB: Customer meters in the area are reading more accurately
optionC: A new leak or an increase in background leakage is likely in the area
optionD: Storage in the area is turning over faster
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: District Metered Areas. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Before trusting district metered area night flow data, what must an operator verify about the boundary?
correctAnswer: That boundary valves are closed and not passing, and all inflows are metered
explanation: If a boundary valve passes or an inflow is unmetered, the recorded flow does not represent the area and conclusions will be wrong.
options: That every customer in the area has a new meter
That hydrants in the area have been painted recently
That the area has only one pipe material
That boundary valves are closed and not passing, and all inflows are metered
optionA: That every customer in the area has a new meter
optionB: That hydrants in the area have been painted recently
optionC: That the area has only one pipe material
optionD: That boundary valves are closed and not passing, and all inflows are metered
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: District Metered Areas. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A step test is planned inside a district metered area to locate a leak. How is a step test carried out?
correctAnswer: Sections of the area are isolated one at a time at night while the change in inflow is recorded
explanation: Isolating sections in sequence and watching the flow drop shows which section contains the loss.
options: Pressure is raised in steps until a main breaks
Sections of the area are isolated one at a time at night while the change in inflow is recorded
Customer meters are read in steps from largest to smallest
Chlorine dose is increased in steps and residuals are compared
optionA: Pressure is raised in steps until a main breaks
optionB: Sections of the area are isolated one at a time at night while the change in inflow is recorded
optionC: Customer meters are read in steps from largest to smallest
optionD: Chlorine dose is increased in steps and residuals are compared
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: District Metered Areas. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Two district metered areas have similar customer counts. Area A has much higher night flow per connection than Area B. What is the most reasonable next step?
correctAnswer: Prioritise leak detection work in Area A
explanation: Comparing night flow between similar areas highlights where leakage effort will recover the most water.
options: Replace all customer meters in Area B
Raise pressure in Area A to find the leak faster
Prioritise leak detection work in Area A
Remove Area B from the monitoring program
optionA: Replace all customer meters in Area B
optionB: Raise pressure in Area A to find the leak faster
optionC: Prioritise leak detection work in Area A
optionD: Remove Area B from the monitoring program
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: District Metered Areas. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: On a pump station graph, where does a pump actually operate?
correctAnswer: At the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve
explanation: The operating point is where the head the pump produces equals the head the system requires at that flow.
options: At the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve
At the highest point of the pump curve
At the point of best efficiency in all conditions
At the shutoff head of the pump
optionA: At the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve
optionB: At the highest point of the pump curve
optionC: At the point of best efficiency in all conditions
optionD: At the shutoff head of the pump
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pump Curves And System Curves. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A system curve becomes steeper after a partially closed valve adds resistance. What happens to the operating point of a fixed speed pump?
correctAnswer: Flow decreases and the pump produces higher head
explanation: More system resistance moves the intersection up and to the left on the pump curve, giving less flow at higher head.
options: Flow increases and head decreases
Flow decreases and the pump produces higher head
Flow and head both stay the same
The pump runs out to the end of its curve
optionA: Flow increases and head decreases
optionB: Flow decreases and the pump produces higher head
optionC: Flow and head both stay the same
optionD: The pump runs out to the end of its curve
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pump Curves And System Curves. See README for source scope and limitations.
blueprintObjective: Support Systems: Pump Curves And System Curves

question: Static lift in a pumping system increases because the wet well level drops. How does the system curve change?
correctAnswer: It shifts upward, so the pump delivers less flow
explanation: Higher static lift raises the head needed at every flow, shifting the system curve up and reducing the delivered flow.
options: It shifts downward, so the pump delivers more flow
It becomes flatter with no change in flow
It shifts upward, so the pump delivers less flow
It no longer intersects the pump curve at any point
optionA: It shifts downward, so the pump delivers more flow
optionB: It becomes flatter with no change in flow
optionC: It shifts upward, so the pump delivers less flow
optionD: It no longer intersects the pump curve at any point
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pump Curves And System Curves. See README for source scope and limitations.
blueprintObjective: Support Systems: Pump Curves And System Curves

question: Two identical pumps are run in parallel into a common header. Compared with one pump, what does the combination mainly provide?
correctAnswer: More flow at a similar head, limited by the system curve
explanation: Parallel pumps add their flows at the same head, and the actual gain depends on where the combined curve meets the system curve.
options: More flow at a similar head, limited by the system curve
Double the head at the same flow
The same flow with half the energy use
Automatic protection against water hammer
optionA: More flow at a similar head, limited by the system curve
optionB: Double the head at the same flow
optionC: The same flow with half the energy use
optionD: Automatic protection against water hammer
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Pump Curves And System Curves. See README for source scope and limitations.
blueprintObjective: Support Systems: Pump Curves And System Curves

question: A pump is operating far to the right of its best efficiency point. What risk does this create?
correctAnswer: Cavitation, vibration, and accelerated wear from excessive flow
explanation: Running out on the curve raises velocity and net positive suction head required, which can cause cavitation and damage.
options: Loss of prime at the suction eye only
Higher than normal discharge pressure
Freezing of the discharge line in winter
Cavitation, vibration, and accelerated wear from excessive flow
optionA: Loss of prime at the suction eye only
optionB: Higher than normal discharge pressure
optionC: Freezing of the discharge line in winter
optionD: Cavitation, vibration, and accelerated wear from excessive flow

question: Why is regular turnover of treated water storage important for water quality?
correctAnswer: It limits water age, which helps maintain disinfectant residual and limits nitrification risk
explanation: Exchanging stored water regularly keeps water age low, which supports residual and reduces quality deterioration.
options: It increases the pressure available at peak demand
It removes the need to sample storage facilities
It limits water age, which helps maintain disinfectant residual and limits nitrification risk
It prevents corrosion of the tank coating directly
optionA: It increases the pressure available at peak demand
optionB: It removes the need to sample storage facilities
optionC: It limits water age, which helps maintain disinfectant residual and limits nitrification risk
optionD: It prevents corrosion of the tank coating directly
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Storage Turnover Management. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A standpipe is operated in a narrow level band near the top. What is the likely water quality concern?
correctAnswer: Only a small portion of the stored volume is exchanged, so much of the water ages in place
explanation: A narrow operating band exchanges little volume each cycle, leaving older water stored for long periods.
options: Only a small portion of the stored volume is exchanged, so much of the water ages in place
The overflow will operate continuously
The tank will drain completely during peak demand
Inlet chlorine will be overdosed at low levels
optionA: Only a small portion of the stored volume is exchanged, so much of the water ages in place
optionB: The overflow will operate continuously
optionC: The tank will drain completely during peak demand
optionD: Inlet chlorine will be overdosed at low levels
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Storage Turnover Management. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Which operating change most directly increases daily turnover in an elevated tank?
correctAnswer: Widening the daily drawdown and refill range used by the level controls
explanation: Turnover depends on the volume exchanged each day, and a wider level swing exchanges more water.
options: Raising the overflow elevation of the tank
Painting the tank a lighter colour
Sampling the tank more frequently each week
Widening the daily drawdown and refill range used by the level controls
optionA: Raising the overflow elevation of the tank
optionB: Painting the tank a lighter colour
optionC: Sampling the tank more frequently each week
optionD: Widening the daily drawdown and refill range used by the level controls
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Storage Turnover Management. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: In cold climate operation, why might operators limit how far a storage tank is drawn down in winter?
correctAnswer: To reduce ice formation and protect inlet and outlet piping from freezing problems
explanation: Ice management is a real constraint in western Canadian winters, and level strategy balances turnover against freezing risk.
options: To keep chlorine residual as high as possible
To reduce ice formation and protect inlet and outlet piping from freezing problems
To avoid using the altitude valve in winter
To increase water age during cold months
optionA: To keep chlorine residual as high as possible
optionB: To reduce ice formation and protect inlet and outlet piping from freezing problems
optionC: To avoid using the altitude valve in winter
optionD: To increase water age during cold months
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Storage Turnover Management. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Residual at a tank outlet has fallen while the inlet residual is normal. The tank level record shows little change for several days. What is the most likely cause?
correctAnswer: Poor turnover has allowed the stored water to age and lose residual
explanation: Stagnant stored water loses residual over time, and the flat level record confirms little exchange occurred.
options: Poor turnover has allowed the stored water to age and lose residual
The inlet sample tap is faulty
The tank has been bypassed by a closed valve
A cross connection is adding chlorine to the tank
optionA: Poor turnover has allowed the stored water to age and lose residual
optionB: The inlet sample tap is faulty
optionC: The tank has been bypassed by a closed valve
optionD: A cross connection is adding chlorine to the tank
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Storage Turnover Management. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: In a chloraminated system, which set of results most strongly suggests nitrification is starting in a storage tank?
correctAnswer: Falling total chlorine with rising nitrite and falling free ammonia
explanation: Nitrifying bacteria consume free ammonia and produce nitrite while chloramine decays, so that combination is the classic early signal.
options: Rising total chlorine with rising alkalinity
Falling turbidity with rising pH
Rising nitrite with rising total chlorine
Falling total chlorine with rising nitrite and falling free ammonia
optionA: Rising total chlorine with rising alkalinity
optionB: Falling turbidity with rising pH
optionC: Rising nitrite with rising total chlorine
optionD: Falling total chlorine with rising nitrite and falling free ammonia
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Nitrification Monitoring And Response. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: What is usually the first operational response when early nitrification is confirmed in one storage facility?
correctAnswer: Increase turnover of that facility and remove it from service for cleaning or flushing if needed
explanation: Exchanging the aged water and, where needed, cleaning the facility removes the conditions and the bacterial population driving nitrification.
options: Add more ammonia at the treatment plant
Increase turnover of that facility and remove it from service for cleaning or flushing if needed
Lower the finished water pH sharply
Stop all sampling until residuals recover
optionA: Add more ammonia at the treatment plant
optionB: Increase turnover of that facility and remove it from service for cleaning or flushing if needed
optionC: Lower the finished water pH sharply
optionD: Stop all sampling until residuals recover
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Nitrification Monitoring And Response. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Why does warm weather increase nitrification risk in a distribution system?
correctAnswer: Nitrifying bacteria grow faster at warmer temperatures, especially in aged water
explanation: Temperature speeds bacterial growth, so summer water age problems appear sooner and progress faster.
options: Chloramine forms more quickly in warm water
Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen at all times
Nitrifying bacteria grow faster at warmer temperatures, especially in aged water
Customer demand always falls in warm weather
optionA: Chloramine forms more quickly in warm water
optionB: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen at all times
optionC: Nitrifying bacteria grow faster at warmer temperatures, especially in aged water
optionD: Customer demand always falls in warm weather
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Nitrification Monitoring And Response. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A utility monitors free ammonia at distribution sites. What does a steady decline in free ammonia at one site, with stable plant dosing, suggest?
correctAnswer: Ammonia is being consumed in that part of the system, consistent with nitrification activity
explanation: Free ammonia is the food source for nitrifying bacteria, so local consumption points to biological activity at or upstream of the site.
options: The plant analysers are over reading ammonia
Too much chlorine is being added at the plant
The site has developed a cross connection
Ammonia is being consumed in that part of the system, consistent with nitrification activity
optionA: The plant analysers are over reading ammonia
optionB: Too much chlorine is being added at the plant
optionC: The site has developed a cross connection
optionD: Ammonia is being consumed in that part of the system, consistent with nitrification activity
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Nitrification Monitoring And Response. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: Which practice best prevents nitrification episodes across a whole chloraminated system?
correctAnswer: Managing water age through turnover, flushing of low use areas, and a stable chloramine residual
explanation: Nitrification is driven by age, warmth, and available ammonia, so system wide age and residual management is the preventive control.
options: Keeping all storage tanks as full as possible at all times
Managing water age through turnover, flushing of low use areas, and a stable chloramine residual
Sampling only at the treatment plant outlet
Raising ammonia dose whenever temperature rises
optionA: Keeping all storage tanks as full as possible at all times
optionB: Managing water age through turnover, flushing of low use areas, and a stable chloramine residual
optionC: Sampling only at the treatment plant outlet
optionD: Raising ammonia dose whenever temperature rises
sourceReference: Supporting topic reference: Nitrification Monitoring And Response. See README for source scope and limitations.

question: A valve exercising program records a valve that will not fully close during an emergency isolation trial. What is the correct program response?
correctAnswer: Document the deficiency, schedule repair or replacement, and note the isolation risk in the records used by crews
explanation: A valve that cannot close changes how an emergency isolation would be done, so the deficiency and its risk must be recorded and corrected.
options: Remove the valve from the asset register
Leave the valve half open so it stays movable
Document the deficiency, schedule repair or replacement, and note the isolation risk in the records used by crews
Rely on the next valve in line without recording the issue

optionB: Leave the valve half open so it stays movable
optionC: Document the deficiency, schedule repair or replacement, and note the isolation risk in the records used by crews
optionD: Rely on the next valve in line without recording the issue

question: During hydrant inspections, a hydrant is found with a damaged cap and water sitting inside the barrel in late autumn. Why is prompt drainage or repair a priority in a cold climate?
correctAnswer: Trapped water can freeze, damaging the hydrant and taking it out of service when it may be needed
explanation: Freeze damage is a leading cold climate hydrant failure, and a barrel that does not drain is a known warning sign.
options: Trapped water can freeze, damaging the hydrant and taking it out of service when it may be needed
A wet barrel raises the chlorine residual nearby
Caps are required for hydrant flow testing only
Standing water increases hydrant paint life

optionD: Standing water increases hydrant paint life

question: A supervisor reviews valve program data and finds one area has many valves recorded as located but not operated for years. What is the best use of this finding?
correctAnswer: Prioritise that area in the exercising schedule because untested valves are an isolation risk
explanation: Program data should drive risk based scheduling, and long unoperated valves are the highest isolation risk.
options: Cancel exercising there because the valves are undisturbed
Prioritise that area in the exercising schedule because untested valves are an isolation risk
Replace every valve in the area immediately
Transfer the area to the hydrant program only

question: A hydrant flow test program and a valve program share field crews. Which record linkage gives the most value for planning main replacement?
correctAnswer: Combining hydrant flow results showing poor capacity with valve condition records for the same streets

Matching the number of hydrants tested to the number of staff on shift
Combining hydrant flow results showing poor capacity with valve condition records for the same streets
Recording only the hydrants that pass each year

question: Before a planned shutdown for a main repair, what should the program records be used to confirm?
correctAnswer: That every valve in the isolation plan has been located, is accessible, and has operated successfully in recent records
explanation: Shutdowns fail when an assumed valve cannot be found or operated, so recent verified records are checked before the work is scheduled.
options: That every valve in the isolation plan has been located, is accessible, and has operated successfully in recent records
That all hydrants in the city were inspected this year
That customer meters near the repair are newly installed
That the repair crew holds confined space training only

question: Why do utilities prioritise testing of large customer meters over small residential meters?
correctAnswer: A small percentage error on a large meter affects a large volume of billed water and revenue
explanation: Large meters pass high volumes, so even modest under registration represents significant non revenue water and lost revenue.
options: Large meters are always less accurate than small meters
Large meters are not read by the billing system
Residential meters never lose accuracy with age
A small percentage error on a large meter affects a large volume of billed water and revenue

question: A large meter is tested at high, medium, and low flow rates. It is accurate at high flow but under registers badly at low flow. What does this pattern suggest?
correctAnswer: Wear or damage that affects the measuring element most at low flows, common in older mechanical meters
explanation: Mechanical wear shows first at low flow, where friction and clearances have the largest relative effect on registration.
options: The meter is oversized for the service and should be left alone
The test bench is inaccurate at all flow rates
Wear or damage that affects the measuring element most at low flows, common in older mechanical meters
The customer is using water only at night

optionD: The customer is using water only at night

question: A large meter consistently under registers. Apparent losses in the water balance will be affected in which way?
correctAnswer: Apparent losses will be overstated because billed consumption is recorded lower than actual use
explanation: Under registration lowers recorded consumption, and the water balance assigns that gap to losses even though the water was used.
options: Apparent losses will be overstated because billed consumption is recorded lower than actual use
Apparent losses will be understated by the same amount
Real losses will increase by the meter error volume
The water balance will be unaffected by meter error
optionA: Apparent losses will be overstated because billed consumption is recorded lower than actual use
optionB: Apparent losses will be understated by the same amount
optionC: Real losses will increase by the meter error volume

question: When selecting which large meters to test first, which factor should carry the most weight?
correctAnswer: The volume of water passing through the meter combined with its age and test history
explanation: Testing effort returns the most value where throughput is high and accuracy is most in doubt from age or history.
options: The colour of the meter register head
The distance from the meter shop to the site
Whether the customer has complained about bills
The volume of water passing through the meter combined with its age and test history
optionA: The colour of the meter register head
optionB: The distance from the meter shop to the site
